### Cooperation attenuates the costs of cheating in large groups

The consequences of cheating for hatching success depended on the number of cooperators, and operated through complete nest failure rather than through a gradual reduction in the proportion of hatched eggs. In groups containing a cheat, the probability that a nest failed dropped steeply as the number of cooperators increased (PM (CI) = `r st_nest_failure[st_nest_failure$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - Yes : ZNumber of cooperators","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_nest_failure[st_nest_failure$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - Yes : ZNumber of cooperators","pMCMC"]`), whereas in groups without cheats it was unrelated to the number of cooperators (PM (CI) = `r st_nest_failure[st_nest_failure$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of cooperators","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_nest_failure[st_nest_failure$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of cooperators","pMCMC"]`); the two slopes differed significantly (PM (CI) = `r st_nest_failure[st_nest_failure$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of cooperators vs Cheat in camp - Yes : ZNumber of cooperators","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_nest_failure[st_nest_failure$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of cooperators vs Cheat in camp - Yes : ZNumber of cooperators","pMCMC"]`; Fig. 4A. Extended Data Table 13). All `r words(nrow(df_hatching[df_hatching$FCheatinCamp == "Yes" & df_hatching$noFCoopsCamp == 1,]))` groups containing a cheat and a single cooperator failed completely, hatching none of their `r sum(df_hatching$no.eggsCampInc[df_hatching$FCheatinCamp == "Yes" & df_hatching$noFCoopsCamp == 1])` eggs, whereas every group with a cheat and four or five cooperators successfully produced one or more offspring. Among nests that produced offspring, the proportion of eggs that hatched did not differ between groups with and without cheats (PM (CI) = `r st_hatch_success[st_hatch_success$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No vs Cheat in camp - Yes","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_hatch_success[st_hatch_success$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No vs Cheat in camp - Yes","pMCMC"]`) and did not vary differently with the number of cooperators (PM (CI) = `r st_hatch_success[st_hatch_success$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of cooperators vs Cheat in camp - Yes : ZNumber of cooperators","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_hatch_success[st_hatch_success$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of cooperators vs Cheat in camp - Yes : ZNumber of cooperators","pMCMC"]`; Fig. 4B. Extended Data Table 13). These results indicate that cheating did not incrementally influence hatching success, but was instead associated with complete nest failure when there were few cooperators.

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=F, fig.cap = paste0("**Figure 4: Complete hatching failure occurred in small groups with cheats.** (A) Percentage of nests producing no offspring in groups with (orange) and without (green) cheats as a function of the number of cooperators. Circle area is proportional to the number of groups with vertical lines showing 95% Wilson binomial confidence intervals. (B) Hatching success among nests that produced at least one offspring. Circles and error bars show means ± one standard error. Solid lines show fitted values from Bayesian generalised linear mixed models (Extended Data Table 13); shaded ribbons show 95% credible intervals.", " Sample sizes: (A) n = ", nrow(df_nest_failure), " groups; (B) n = ", nrow(df_hatch_success), " groups, those that hatched at least one egg."), fig.height = 9.5, fig.width = 9, dpi = 600, align = "center"}
#**Model predictions for Figure 4 (fitted lines +/- 95% credible intervals)*
#Hatching success is modelled in two parts (Model 11). Panel A is the probability that a nest hatched
#no eggs (m_nest_failure_int_c1, binomial / logit link) and panel B the proportion of eggs hatching among nests that
#hatched at least one (m_hatch_success_int_c1, binomial / logit link). Both are population-average (marginal) fits,
#averaged over the random effects so they are comparable to the plotted group means, with the number of
#"other" females held at its mean. The marginal mean is plogis(lp / sqrt(1 + c^2 * V)) with
#c = 16*sqrt(3)/(15*pi) and V the total random-effect variance per posterior sample; results are
#expressed as percentages. Number of cooperators was z-transformed before modelling.
coop11_mean <- mean(df_nest_failure$noFCoopsCamp)
coop11_sd   <- sd(df_nest_failure$noFCoopsCamp)
logit_c     <- 16 * sqrt(3) / (15 * pi)
coop11_grid <- seq(1, 5, by = 0.05)
#Fitted values for one cheat-presence group across the plotted range, for either part of the model.
#Returns a probability on the 0-1 scale; panel B converts it to a percentage.
fitted_hurdle <- function(model, L, x, zOther){
  z  <- (x - coop11_mean) / coop11_sd
  lp <- model$Sol[, paste0("FCheatinCamp", L)] + model$Sol[, "ZnoFOther"] * zOther +
        model$Sol[, paste0("FCheatinCamp", L, ":ZnoFCoops")] * z
  plogis(lp / sqrt(1 + logit_c^2 * rowSums(model$VCV)))
}
df_nest_failure_fit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("No", "Yes"), function(L) do.call(rbind, lapply(coop11_grid, function(x){
  p <- fitted_hurdle(m_nest_failure_int_c1, L, x, mean(df_nest_failure$ZnoFOther))
  data.frame(FCheatinCamp = L, noFCoopsCamp = x, mean = median(p), lcl = quantile(p, 0.025), ucl = quantile(p, 0.975))}))))
#Panel B is plotted as a percentage, so the fitted probabilities are multiplied by 100 here
df_hatch_success_fit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("No", "Yes"), function(L) do.call(rbind, lapply(coop11_grid, function(x){
  p <- fitted_hurdle(m_hatch_success_int_c1, L, x, mean(df_hatch_success$ZnoFOther)) * 100
  data.frame(FCheatinCamp = L, noFCoopsCamp = x, mean = median(p), lcl = quantile(p, 0.025), ucl = quantile(p, 0.975))}))))
#
#**Observed values*
#Panel A shows the proportion of groups that hatched nothing, with 95% Wilson binomial intervals, which
#unlike a standard error behave sensibly at 0 and 1 and when only a few groups contribute.
#The interval is computed with pmax/pmin over whole columns rather than row by row: Rmisc loads plyr,
#whose mutate() masks dplyr's and silently ignores rowwise(), which would otherwise collapse the
#interval to a single value recycled across every group size.
Fig5aSum <- df_nest_failure %>% group_by(noFCoopsCamp, FCheatinCamp) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(n = n(), k = sum(failed), pct = mean(failed), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(wilson_p    = k / n,
                wilson_den  = 1 + 1.96^2 / n,
                wilson_hw   = 1.96 * sqrt(wilson_p * (1 - wilson_p) / n + 1.96^2 / (4 * n^2)),
                lcl = pmax(0, (wilson_p + 1.96^2 / (2 * n) - wilson_hw) / wilson_den),
                ucl = pmin(1, (wilson_p + 1.96^2 / (2 * n) + wilson_hw) / wilson_den)) %>%
  dplyr::select(-wilson_p, -wilson_den, -wilson_hw)
Fig5bDat <- df_hatch_success %>% mutate(hatch_pct = 100 * no.HatchedInc / no.eggsCampInc)
Fig5bSum <- Fig5bDat %>% group_by(noFCoopsCamp, FCheatinCamp) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(hatch_pct),
                   se = ifelse(n() > 1, sd(hatch_pct)/sqrt(n()), NA_real_), .groups = "drop")
#
Fig5a <- ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = df_nest_failure_fit, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl, fill = FCheatinCamp), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(data = df_nest_failure_fit, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, y = mean, colour = FCheatinCamp), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_linerange(data = Fig5aSum, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl, colour = FCheatinCamp),
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.3), linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = Fig5aSum, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, y = pct, fill = FCheatinCamp, size = n),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.3), shape = 21, colour = "black", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Yes" = "#E69F00", "No" = "#009E73"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Yes" = "#E69F00", "No" = "#009E73"), name = "Cheat present") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2.2, 7), name = "No. groups") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "No. of cooperators in group", y = "Probability of nest failure") + t1 +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14), axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14))
#
Fig5b <- ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = df_hatch_success_fit, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl, fill = FCheatinCamp), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(data = df_hatch_success_fit, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, y = mean, colour = FCheatinCamp), linewidth = 1) +
  #Individual groups behind the means
  geom_point(data = Fig5bDat, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, y = hatch_pct, colour = FCheatinCamp),
  position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.28, dodge.width = 0.3, seed = 1), alpha = 0.3, size = 1.3) +
  geom_pointrange(data = Fig5bSum, aes(x = noFCoopsCamp, y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se, fill = FCheatinCamp),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.3), shape = 21, colour = "black", size = 0.55, fatten = 6, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Yes" = "#E69F00", "No" = "#009E73"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Yes" = "#E69F00", "No" = "#009E73"), name = "Cheat present") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(x = "No. of cooperators in group", y = "Hatching success (%)\nof nests producing offspring") + t1 +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14), axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14))
#
ggarrange(Fig5a, Fig5b, labels = c("A", "B"), ncol = 1, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "top")
#
```

 

## **Discussion**

Despite cheating occurring across diverse taxa, the conditions under which it can persist without driving cooperation to collapse remain unclear [@west2021a]. Our results show that cheats maximize their reproductive success in large groups, where they are relatively rare, suggesting that the public goods provided by cooperators, principally incubation of the communal nest, allow cheating to proliferate (Fig. 2A). This relationship appears to involve a threshold, where the costs imposed by cheats are minimised when two cooperators or more are present in groups (Fig. 2A & 4A). Individual strategies were also highly flexible, with females adjusting whether they cheated or cooperated in response to their social environment. This flexibility suggests that cheating is not a fixed individual strategy but an emergent and persistent feature of ostrich societies.

These findings are consistent with theory predicting that cheats and cooperators can coexist when the fitness of cheats is negatively frequency-dependent and enough cooperators are present to buffer the costs of cheating[@doebeli_evolutionary_2004; @archetti_review_2012]. Support for this prediction comes mainly from experimental work on microorganisms, where cheating is typically studied as a genetically determined, relatively fixed phenotype[@ross-gillespie2007b; @gore2009a; @lujan2015; @patel2019; @foster2007; @asfahl2017], although facultative cheating has been described[@santorelli_facultative_2008]. The conditional cheating observed here may strengthen negative frequency dependence beyond what fixed strategies produce, because individuals can exploit cooperative groups when cheats are rare and avoid the costs of cheating in less favourable social environments. The same logic underlies the flexible tactics of producer–scrounger games[@barnard_producers_1981; @giraldeau_social_2000] and the conditional parasitism of communal nests in the cooperatively breeding greater ani, *Crotophaga major*[@riehlSocialParasitismAlternative2019].

The primary behavioural mechanism underlying our results is reduced incubation effort, and in some cases apparent desertion by cooperators in small groups containing cheats. Abandoning incubation likely harms cooperators' current reproductive success, given they have invested eggs in nests. However, individuals are expected to base investment decisions on anticipated future benefits rather than sunk past investments[@sargentParentalInvestmentDecision1985], resulting in a trade-off between the immediate costs of desertion and the potential for future reproductive success [@williams1966a; @mcnamara2004; @nielsenIntraspecificNestParasitism2006]. Ostriches are long-lived and breed over many years[@bertram1992a], so the chances of reproducing in the future are likely high. At the same time, the costs of compensating for others’ reduced effort can be substantial, as they are often exposed to extreme temperatures and intense predation pressure[@magigeBreedingBiologyOstriches2009; @bertram1992a; @schou2021a]. Reducing investment in breeding attempts where cheats elevate current costs at the expense of future reproduction may therefore represent an adaptive response in long-lived species.

The cues that female ostriches use to detect cheats remain unknown. Because egg laying and incubation overlap (Fig. 2C), a female's failure to incubate may only become apparent once incubation has begun. Consistent with this, cooperators reduced their incubation effort in response to cheats mainly later in incubation (Fig. 3B). This suggests that cooperators respond to the behaviour of other females during early incubation rather than to egg laying itself. Non-breeding females, which neither laid eggs nor incubated (classified as *other*), provide an indirect test of this idea. In groups without cheats, cooperators incubated less as the number of non-breeding females increased (PM (CI) = `r st_incubation_individual[st_incubation_individual$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of other","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_incubation_individual[st_incubation_individual$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheat in camp - No : ZNumber of other","pMCMC"]`. Extended Data Table 12). This suggests that cooperators adjust their incubation to the number of females that do not incubate, without necessarily distinguishing cheats from other non-contributors. Such a rule requires no recognition of individuals or eggs. Comparably simple rules reduce the costs of parasitism in other communally breeding birds. For example, greater anis (*Crotophaga major*) eject eggs laid later than the rest of the clutch, which removes most parasitic eggs without the need to recognise them [@riehl2010].

In summary, by experimentally allocating individuals to groups of different sizes, our study identifies the conditions under which cheating can persist in a vertebrate cooperative system without causing its collapse. Although cheating is often expected to destabilise cooperation, our results suggest that cheats and cooperators can coexist when cheating is expressed conditionally and its benefits decline as cheats become more common. The greater resilience to cheats of groups with more cooperators is consistent with growing evidence that negative frequency-dependent selection can maintain cheating without undermining cooperation[e.g. @ross-gillespie2007b; @babajanyan2026; @ozkaya2018].

## **Methods**

```{r, echo=F, include=F}
#Create a list of groups (yearcamps) that were included in the study after data cleaning
yearcamps = unique(df_strategy_counts$yearcamp)
#
#Create a dataframe with all genotyped eggs that were included in the study
geno_eggs = parentage2012.2018[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$daysfromEggsleft > -29,]
#
#Create a dataframe with all the eggs collected during the study
eggs_collected = eggs2012.2018[which(eggs2012.2018$daysfromEggsleft > -29 & eggs2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & !is.na(eggs2012.2018$yearcamp)),]
```

### Study population

The research was conducted on a captive population of ostriches kept in fenced areas (range: 2400 - 70600 m2, median = 4700 m2) of Karoo habitat at the Oudtshoorn Research Farm, South Africa (33° 38’ 21.5“S, 22° 15’ 17.4”E). The population was established in 1990 with founding individuals from different farms across South Africa. The ostriches in this population are of a farmed breed that is genetically similar to southern African populations [@davids2012a], and are commonly referred to as South African Blacks (*Struthio camelus var. domesticus*). The study included `r length(unique(treatments2012.2018$id[treatments2012.2018$sex == "M" & treatments2012.2018$nofemales != 1]))` male and `r length(unique(treatments2012.2018$id[treatments2012.2018$sex == "F" & treatments2012.2018$nofemales != 1]))` female ostriches of breeding age (range = `r min(treatments2012.2018$age)`-`r max(treatments2012.2018$age)` years) that were allowed to breed in groups between May and December over a seven-year period (2012 to 2018). Birds were fed a balanced ostrich breeder diet (90–120 g protein, 7.5–10.5 MJ metabolisable energy, 26 g calcium, and 6 g phosphorus per kg feed) and *ad libitum* water during the breeding season. 

### Experimental design

We manipulated group composition by experimentally establishing `r length(unique(treatments2012.2018$yearcamp[treatments2012.2018$nofemales != 1]))` groups (10-17 groups per year) with different numbers of males (1 to 3) and females (2 to 6). Not all combinations of male and female group sizes were represented due to constraints on number of birds and enclosures available. Sample size was reduced by the exclusion of 15 groups for the following reasons: i) one or more group members were removed from the group (due to death, injury or aggressive behaviour), and not replaced, within two weeks from the experimental onset of natural incubation (see *Egg collection and incubation* section below. n~groups~ = `r length(unique(treatments2012.2018$yearcamp[treatments2012.2018$Removal.replacement.score == 4 & treatments2012.2018$nofemales != 1 & !is.na(treatments2012.2018$Removal.replacement.score)]))`); ii) no eggs were laid in the group during the time incubation was monitored (n~groups~ = `r nrow(camps2012.2018[camps2012.2018$no.eggsCampInc == 0 & camps2012.2018$nofemales != 1,])`); iii) no females were observed incubating in the group (n~groups~ = `r nrow(camps2012.2018[camps2012.2018$Ftotsit == 0 & camps2012.2018$nofemales != 1 & camps2012.2018$no.eggsCampInc != 0,])`); and iv) it was not possible to obtain any genetic samples for parentage analysis from the group (n~groups~ = `r nrow(camps2012.2018[camps2012.2018$totGenoeggsCampInc4 == 0 & camps2012.2018$nofemales != 1 & camps2012.2018$no.eggsCampInc != 0,])`). This resulted in a final sample of `r length(unique(df_females$yearcamp))` groups, `r length(unique(inds_filtered_M$id))` males, and `r length(unique(inds_filtered$id))` females. Of these, `r sum(table(inds_filtered_M$id) > 1)` males and `r sum(table(inds_filtered$id) > 1)` females were included in multiple years.

### Classification of breeding strategies

Females were classified as *cooperators*, *cheats* or *other* depending on whether they laid eggs in the nest and whether they contributed to incubation. *Cooperators* were females that contributed to incubation, regardless of whether they laid eggs in the nest or not. *Cheats* laid eggs in the nest, but did not incubate. *Other* females did not lay any eggs or contribute to incubation. We estimated individual egg laying through genetic parentage analyses of a sample of eggs and chicks (see *Genetic determination of parentage* below). Incubation bouts of one minute or less were excluded to avoid recording egg-laying behaviour as incubation. As a complete site scan required approximately three minutes, individuals with three or less minutes of cumulative incubation time across the season were classified as non-incubators, preventing classification based on a single brief detection.

### Measuring reproduction
#### Egg collection and incubation

During the first approximate five months of the experiment, eggs were collected from nests twice a day and incubated artificially. Each egg was marked with the time of collection and group identity, and exposed to UV light for 20 minutes for disinfection. Eggs were incubated in weekly batches, and prior to incubation they were stored for 1–6 days under conditions that maintain hatching success [@brand2008b]: placed on turning trays (two daily 180° rotations) in a cold room (17°C) with relative humidity between 80% and 90%. Eggs were transferred to incubators set at 36.2°C and a relative humidity of 24% with automatic rotation of 60° around their long axis every hour. At day 39 of incubation, eggs were moved to hatching cabinets and thereafter inspected daily for signs of pipping.

During the final approximate 50 days of the experiment (mean = 47; range = 23-61 days), eggs were no longer collected, and birds were allowed to incubate naturally. This phase, referred to as the "incubation period", allowed us to monitor the natural incubation behaviour of females. During the incubation period, nests were checked daily, and newly laid eggs were marked with the date and a unique egg identification number. The presence or absence of previously laid eggs was recorded to track the fate of each egg. In the first three years (2012–2014), birds were allowed to incubate eggs through to hatching. If no hatching was observed after 50 days of incubation, eggs were removed. From 2015 onwards, contact between adults and chicks had to be reduced following legislation aimed at reducing the spread of avian flu. Eggs were removed from nests just before the anticipated hatching date, approximately 40 days after the onset of the incubation period, and placed in artificial incubators to determine hatching success. In 2018, egg theft meant that groups had to restart their clutches and eggs had to be removed after 28 days, instead of 40 days, when birds were removed from their breeding enclosures.

#### Genetic determination of parentage

Blood samples were collected from adults prior to being placed in experimental groups and their offspring at hatching. Unhatched eggs were dissected to obtain blood or tissue samples. All procedures were approved by the Departmental Ethics Committee for Research on Animals (DECRA) of the Western Cape Department of Agriculture (project no. AP/BR/O/SC14).

During the first three years of the study (2012–2014), parentage of `r nrow(parentage2012.2018[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year < 2015,])` offspring was determined using seven highly polymorphic microsatellites previously shown to assign parentage with high confidence in ostriches [@bonato_investment_2009]. The number of samples genotyped per group was chosen to be proportional to the number of females in the group (aiming for 10 samples per female where possible), spread across the breeding season (range of samples per group = `r min(table(parentage2012.2018$yearcamp[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year < 2015]))`–`r max(table(parentage2012.2018$yearcamp[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year < 2015]))`). See Melgar et al., 2022 [@melgar2022] for details on the microsatellite protocol for parentage analysis.

In the final four years of the study (2015–2018), parentage was determined using single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from up to `r max(table(parentage2012.2018$yearcamp[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year > 2014]))` offspring per group (we targeted 20 eggs during the artificial incubation phase, and 20 eggs during the natural incubation phase. Total samples = `r nrow(parentage2012.2018[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year > 2014,])`, range of samples per group = `r min(table(parentage2012.2018$yearcamp[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year > 2014]))`–`r max(table(parentage2012.2018$yearcamp[parentage2012.2018$yearcamp %in% yearcamps & parentage2012.2018$year > 2014]))`). See Melgar et al., 2022 [@melgar2022] for details on DNA extraction, identification of markers, and parentage analysis using SNPs.

#### Individual reproductive success

Genetic parentage data from eggs laid during the incubation period were used to estimate the reproductive success of individual females. However, as egg laying rates decline during incubation, and many eggs are broken when left in the nests [@melgar2022], parentage sample sizes from the incubation period were low. We therefore included eggs from the 28 days prior to the onset of incubation, which produced a more reliable estimate of the females that laid eggs in each group. This period of 28 days prior to the onset of incubation together with the incubation period is refereed to as the "laying period".

The estimated number of eggs laid by an individual provided a proxy for reproductive success. To account for between-year variation, this value was then divided by the mean number of eggs laid by females in the same year, referred to as *relative number of eggs* in the paper.

### Group reproductive success

The reproductive output of groups was measured as the number of eggs produced during the incubation period. Group-level hatching success was defined as the percentage of these eggs that hatched, either in the nest or in artificial incubators.

### Monitoring incubation behaviour

Incubation behaviour was monitored through approximately three-hour observations at least three times per week using binoculars (10 x 40) and a telescope (20-60 x 80). Three observers rotated shifts from a camouflaged 10 m observation tower in the center of the groups. Each group was observed for 47 to 91 hours in total. Individual incubation effort was defined as the proportion of time each individual spent incubating (total time observed incubating divided by total observation time). Individuals were identified by colour-tags.

### Monitoring aggressive behaviour

Aggressive interactions between females were recorded during observation sessions using the following classifications: 1) hissing or grunting against another individual; 2) 1 + pursuing with lifted wings; 3) 2 + trotting and chasing; 4) 2 + running and chasing; 5) 2 + chasing by persistently sprinting; 6) kicking.

### Statistical analyses
#### General approach

Data were analysed in R using Bayesian Linear Mixed Models (BLMM) with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation in the package MCMCglmm[@hadfieldMCMCglmmCourseNotes2021]. For all non-binary response variable models, we used default fixed effect priors (independent normal priors with zero mean and large variance of 10^10^) and inverse gamma priors for random effects. For binary response variable models, fixed effect priors were specified as mu = 0, V = 1 + π2 / 3 (relatively flat on the logit scale), while parameter expanded priors were used for random effects (V = 1, nu = 0.002, alpha.mu = 0, alpha.V = 1000)[@hadfieldMCMCglmmCourseNotes2021]. The residual variance was fixed at 1 in binary models as it is not identifiable. Each analysis was run for 2000000 iterations with a burn-in of 200000 and a thinning interval of 500, retaining 3600 samples per chain. A random number seed was set before each model was fitted, so that every analysis reported here is exactly reproducible from the archived code. Convergence was checked by running models three times and visually examining the overlap of traces, levels of autocorrelation, and Gelman and Rubin’s convergence diagnostic (potential scale reduction factors <1.1 support model convergence).

Fixed effects estimates were reported from models that included all terms of the same order and lower: all main-effect estimates are from models containing all other main effects, estimates of two-way interactions are from models including all two-way interactions and main effects, and so forth. Continuous explanatory variables were z-standardised (zero-centred with unit standard deviation) using the scale() function in R, if nothing else is specified. Curvilinear relationships were modelled using the quadratic terms that were computed from the z-standardised predictors before running the models. Quadratic terms were tested in models that included main effects, other quadratic effects and two-way interactions.

Effect magnitudes were quantified using model coefficients and, where specified, posterior contrasts between coefficients. Fixed-effect coefficients and their contrasts are reported as posterior modes with 95% highest-posterior-density credible intervals (CIs), on the model’s linear-predictor scale. A fixed effect was considered significant when its 95% CI did not overlap with 0 and pMCMC was less than 0.05. Two-sided pMCMC values were calculated as twice the smaller of the proportions of posterior samples greater than zero and less than or equal to zero, with a minimum value of 1/N, where N is the number of retained posterior samples. To obtain absolute estimates and 95% CIs for each factor level and to facilitate custom contrasts between levels, we removed the global intercept from all models with fixed factors (unless otherwise specified below) and present absolute estimates. Differences between factor levels were estimated by subtracting corresponding posterior samples between levels and calculating the posterior mode, 95% CI, and pMCMC. Non-independence due to multiple data points per individual, group, camp (enclosure used repeatedly across years), and year was accounted for using random effects. The magnitude of random effects was quantified by calculating the percentage of variation explained by each random term (I2%: (Vi/V~total~)x100, where V~total~ is the sum of the random-effect and residual variance components)[@devillemereuilGeneralMethodsEvolutionary2016] after accounting for variation attributable to fixed effects. To account for distribution-specific variance, this variance was included in the denominator (Vi/(V~total~ + Vd) x100), where Vd is π2/3 for binomial models with a logit link, 1 for models with a probit link, and ln(1 + 1/λ) for Poisson models with a log link, with λ the fitted mean on the data scale. Random effect estimates are reported from models that included the highest order fixed effect terms.

Most breeding groups contained a single communal nest, but in `r sum(df_strategy_counts$nonests[df_strategy_counts$BS == "Cheat"] == 2)` of the `r length(unique(df_strategy_counts$yearcamp))` groups a second nest was present. Additional nests resulted when more than one male dug a nest, when a nest was abandoned and another started, or when individuals laid sporadically outside the primary nest. We therefore included the number of nests in a group as a fixed effect in Models 1 and 2, and found that it had no effect on the frequency of cheating (Extended Data Tables 1 and 2). The number of nests was therefore not included in subsequent analyses.

#### Specific analyses

##### Model 1: Effect of group size on numbers of cheats and cooperators (Extended Data Table 1)

We fitted a model with Poisson error distribution of the counts of individuals adopting different breeding strategies (cheat versus cooperator) within each group. The analysis included `r nrow(df_strategy_counts)` strategy-specific counts from `r length(unique(df_strategy_counts$yearcamp))` breeding groups, with each group contributing one count of cheats and one count of cooperators. Group size was defined as the number of females in the group, including non-breeding females (classified as *other* in later models). We fitted an interaction between breeding strategy and number of females, which allowed us to estimate separate slopes for cheats and cooperators. The number of nests in the group was also included as a fixed effect (see *General approach*). Year, camp and group were included as random effects.

##### Model 2: Effect of group size on the proportion of cheats in groups (Extended Data Table 2)

We modelled the proportion of cheats in relation to cooperators as draws from a binomial distribution with family = “multinomial2”. The response variable was the number of cheating females in each group versus the number of cooperators. The analysis included `r nrow(df_cheat_prop)` breeding groups. Note that group size was modelled with two separate fixed effects: number of cooperators, and number of *other* females. This allowed us to test how the proportion of cheats changed with number of cooperators while controlling the presence of non-breeding females. Number of nests in the group was included as a fixed effect (see *General approach*). As none of the fixed effects were factorial, we kept the global intercept in the model. Year and camp were included as random effects.

##### Model 3: Effects of group composition, age and body mass on cheating probability (Extended Data Table 3)

We modelled the probability of a female being a cheat each year as a binary variable using a Bernoulli error distribution with a probit link function (family = “threshold”). The analysis included `r nrow(df_cheat_prob)` observations of  `r length(unique(df_cheat_prob$id))` females distributed across `r length(unique(df_cheat_prob$yearcamp))` breeding groups. Only females that appeared in more than one year were included in this analysis. We included the number of cooperators (excluding the focal female), and number of *other* females (excluding the focal female) in each group as fixed effects. Excluding the focal female from these ensured that the social environment was defined independently of the focal female’s breeding strategy. Age, and body mass (kg) at the start of the breeding season were included as fixed effects. Year, camp, group and individual were included as random effects. As none of the fixed effects were factorial, we kept the global intercept in the model. 

##### Model 4: Effects of breeding strategy and group composition on end of season body mass (Extended Data Table 4)

We modelled whether cheats and cooperators differed in their body condition at the end of the breeding season by modelling female body mass at the end of incubation with a Gaussian error distribution, fitting breeding strategy together with its interactions with the number of cooperators, the number of *other* females, and body mass at the start of the season as fixed effects. The analysis included `r nrow(df_mass)` observations of `r length(unique(df_mass$id))` females distributed across `r length(unique(df_mass$yearcamp))` breeding groups. Only cheats and cooperators were included in this analysis, and individuals were excluded if they had no recorded start of season body mass (three individuals) or end of season body mass (one individual). Year, camp, group and individual were included as random effects. Cheats and cooperators did not differ in body mass at the end of the season (PM (CI) = `r st_mass[st_mass$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheats vs Cooperators","Posterior Mode (CI)"]`, pMCMC = `r st_mass[st_mass$'Fixed Effects' == "Cheats vs Cooperators","pMCMC"]`. Extended Data Table 4).

##### Model 5: Effect of cheating and group composition on number of eggs laid (Extended Data Table 5)

We modelled the number of eggs females laid each year using a Poisson error distribution with year as a random effect to account for year-to-year differences in the number of eggs laid. The analysis included `r nrow(df_eggs)` observations of `r length(unique(df_eggs$id))` females distributed across `r length(unique(df_eggs$yearcamp))` breeding groups. Only cheats and cooperators were included in this analysis, and since we were interested in comparing number of eggs produced by cheats and cooperators at different number of cooperators per group, groups with six cooperators were excluded (six was the maximum number of females included in a group). We fitted breeding strategy (a three-level factorial effect: 1) Cheats, 2) Cooperator in a group without a cheat, 3) Cooperator in a group with a cheat), number of *other*, and proportion of eggs broken in the nest as fixed effects. To test the effect of group size on egg production of cheats and cooperators, we fitted interactions between breeding strategy and both the linear and quadratic terms of the number of cooperators. Year, camp, group and individual were included as random effects.

We also included a second version of model 5, which was specified in the same way, but data were filtered to exclude groups with only one cooperator (Extended Data Table 5).  This resulted in `r nrow(df_eggs_excl_1coop)` observations of `r length(unique(df_eggs_excl_1coop$id))` females distributed across `r length(unique(df_eggs_excl_1coop$yearcamp))` breeding groups. This additional analysis allowed us to test whether the effects observed in Model 5 were robust to the exclusion of the smallest groups. The results confirmed that groups with only one cooperator were important in explaining the significant effect of cheats on differences in cooperators' reproductive output across group sizes.

##### Model 6: The reproductive success of individuals when they cheat and when they cooperate (Extended Data Table 6)

We modelled the estimated number of eggs produced by females that were both cheats and cooperators across years. We modelled the number of eggs females laid each year using a Poisson error distribution with year as a random effect to account for year-to-year differences in the number of eggs laid. The analysis included `r nrow(df_eggs_within_female)` observations of `r length(unique(df_eggs_within_female$id))` females distributed across `r length(unique(df_eggs_within_female$yearcamp))` breeding groups. Breeding strategy (cheats or cooperates), number of females in the group, and age were included as fixed effects. Only individuals that cheated in some years and cooperated in others were included in this analysis. Year, camp, group and individual were included as random effects.

##### Model 7: Group-level egg laying over time (Extended Data Table 7)

The cumulative proportion of the total number of eggs laid in a nest that were present each day was modelled with a binomial error distribution and logit link function (family = "multinomial2"). The response variable was the eggs laid each day versus the remaining eggs to be laid that season. The analysis included `r nrow(df_laying_group)` observations in `r length(unique(df_laying_group$yearcamp))` groups across `r length(unique(df_laying_group$laydate_date))` observation days. The number of cooperators, number of *other* females, presence of cheats (two-level factorial effect: Yes or No), and the linear and quadratic effects of time in days since the start of the incubation period were included as fixed effects. Interactions between the presence of cheats and both the linear and quadratic effects of time were fitted to test the effect of cheats on the egg-laying patterns across time. Similarly, we fitted interactions between the number of cooperators and both the linear and quadratic effects of time to test the effect of number of cooperators on the temporal patterns of egg-laying. Egg counts were based on the first 32 days of the period with natural incubation, as some years did not have any data for later days (e.g. 2018). Year, camp and group were included as random effects. 

##### Model 8: Effect of breeding strategy on the timing of egg laying (Extended Data Table 8)
We examined whether cheats and cooperators differed in the timing of egg-laying by modelling whether a female laid an egg within a given two-day window of the laying period (ostriches lay at most every second day). We used a binomial error distribution (family = "categorical"). The analysis included `r nrow(df_laying_window)` observations of `r length(unique(df_laying_window$id))` females distributed across `r length(unique(df_laying_window$yearcamp))` groups and `r n_distinct(df_laying_window$year, df_laying_window$Window_2days)` two-day windows. Only cheats and cooperators were included in this analysis. Breeding strategy and the number of females in the group were included as fixed effects, together with interactions between breeding strategy and both the linear and quadratic effects of window position within the laying period. Year, camp, group, and individual were included as random effects.

##### Model 9: Aggression by cooperators (Extended Data Table 9)

To test whether cooperators directed more aggression towards cheats than toward other cooperators, we modelled the number of aggressive interactions initiated by cooperators with a Poisson error distribution. The analysis included `r sum(df_aggression$no.ints)` aggressive interactions (`r sum(df_aggression$no.ints[df_aggression$BSvic == "Cheat"])` against cheats and `r sum(df_aggression$no.ints[df_aggression$BSvic == "Cooperator"])` against cooperators) in `r length(unique(df_aggression$yearcamp))` groups, with each group contributing one count of aggressive interactions against cheats and one count of aggressive interactions against cooperators. Only groups with cheats and with more than one cooperator were included. Victim breeding strategy, observation time, the number of potential victims of the corresponding breeding strategy, and the number of females in the group were fitted as fixed effects, together with an interaction between victim breeding strategy and the number of females. Potential victims were defined as the number of cheats in the group when the victim was a cheat, and as the number of cooperators minus one when the victim was a cooperator, because aggressors were always cooperators and they could not be aggressive towards themselves. For the same reason, groups with only one cooperator were excluded from the analyses. Year, camp, and group were fitted as random effects.

##### Model 10: Effect of cheating and group composition on group-level incubation effort (Extended Data Table 10)

The proportion of time nests were incubated (time incubated vs time not incubated) was modelled with a binomial error distribution and logit link function (family = "multinomial2"). The analysis included the primary nests of `r nrow(df_incubation_group)` groups across `r words(length(unique(df_incubation_group$year)))` years. Since we were interested in comparing incubation effort by groups with and without cheats at different number of cooperators per group, groups with six cooperators (no cheats possible) were excluded. The presence of cheats (Yes or No) was included as a fixed effect along with interactions between presence of cheats and number of cooperators, and between presence of cheats and number of *other* females. Year and camp were included as random effects.

##### Model 11: Effects of cheating on group-level incubation effort over time (Extended Data Table 11)

The proportion of time groups spent incubating each day (incubation time vs time not incubating) was modelled with a binomial error distribution and logit link function (family = "multinomial2"). The analysis included `r nrow(df_incubation_time)` observations in the primary nest of `r length(unique(df_incubation_time$yearcamp))` groups. Only data from the first 32 days of the incubation period each year were included for this analysis, as some years had no observations beyond this time. Only groups where female incubation was recorded during this time were included. We included presence of cheats (Yes or No), number of cooperators, number of *other* females, and the linear and quadratic effects of time (days from onset of incubation period) as fixed effects. We tested the effects of cheating on temporal dynamics of incubation by fitting interactions between the presence of cheats and both the linear and quadratic effects of time. Similarly, we fitted interactions between number of cooperators and both the linear and quadratic effects of time to test if patterns of incubation through time changed in relation of numbers of cooperators. Year, camp and group were included as random effects.

##### Model 12: Effects of cheating, group composition and reproductive investment on individual incubation effort (Extended Data Table 12)

The proportion of time females spent incubating per year (incubation time vs time not incubating) was modelled with a binomial error distribution and logit link function (family = "multinomial2"). The analysis included `r nrow(df_incubation_individual)` individual-year observations of incubations effort from 131 individuals in `r length(unique(df_incubation_individual$yearcamp))` groups. Groups with six cooperators were excluded from this analysis. The presence of cheats (Yes or No) was included as a fixed effect. An interaction between presence of cheats and relative reproductive investment (square root-transformed) was fitted to test whether females adjusted their incubation behaviour in response to cheats depending on the number of eggs they had in the nest. We also fitted interactions between presence of cheats and both the number of *other* females and the number of cooperators. Finally, a three-way interaction between presence of cheats, relative reproductive success and number of cooperators was fitted. Year, camp, group and individual were included as random effects.

##### Model 13: Effect of cheating on hatching success (Extended Data Table 13)

Hatching success was modelled in two parts, because cheating affected whether a nest hatched any eggs at all and the proportion of eggs that hatched among successful nests differently. First, we modelled complete nest failure (no eggs hatched) as a binary response using a binomial error distribution with a logit link. This analysis included nests of `r nrow(df_nest_failure)` groups. The presence of cheats, its interaction with the number of cooperators, and the number of other females were included as fixed effects. Second, among nests that hatched at least one egg (n = `r nrow(df_hatch_success)`), we modelled the number of hatched eggs out of the total number of eggs laid using a binomial error distribution with the same fixed effects. Year and camp were included as random effects in both models. The quadratic of the number of cooperators was investigated but not included in the final model. Every group containing a cheat and a single cooperator failed completely, and because these groups sit at the low end of the cooperator range, they exerted strong leverage on the estimated curvature, producing a predicted decline in hatching success in the largest groups that is not present in the data. Removing single-cooperator groups eliminated the difference in curvature between groups with and without cheats. Groups with six cooperators, where cheating never occurs were excluded from both analyses.


##### Model 14: Effect of cheating on activity allocation of groups (Extended Data Table 14)

We used segmented (breakpoint) regression to test how the allocation of activity between egg-laying and incubation changed over the course of the incubation period (days since the experimental onset of incubation), and whether the timing of the transition between egg-laying and incubation differed depending on whether a cheat was present in the group or not. Activity allocation (act_alloc) was calculated as propsit / (propsit + prop_eggs), where propsit is the proportion of observation time spent incubating (minutes incubating / minutes observed) and prop_eggs is the number of eggs laid by a group during in a given day, divided by the population maximum eggs laid by a group in a day (number of eggs laid / 6). Expressing egg-laying as a proportion, rather than as a raw egg count, placed prop_eggs on the same 0–1 scale as propsit, allowing the two measures to be combined into a single, comparable index of relative activity allocation. This index ranges from 0 (activity allocated entirely to egg-laying) to 1 (activity allocated entirely to incubation).

We used a different statistical framework from the rest of our analyses in this model, as Bayesian MCMC estimation of breakpoint location is not currently supported by available R packages. Instead, models were fitted as linear mixed-effects models in the package *nlme* [@pinheiro2026], with the breakpoint estimated using maximum likelihood via the *segmented* package's extension for mixed models, *segmented.lme* [@muggeo2008; @muggeo2014]. This method estimates the location of a breakpoint in the effect of a continuous predictor together with the change in slope occurring at that point, by iteratively linearizing the breakpoint term and refitting the model until convergence.

Because the *segmented* package does not support bounded proportion-response distributions, we applied a logit transformation to activity allocation (natural log of the odds ratio, using R's *qlogis()* function, with proportions constrained to the interval [0.01, 0.99] to avoid undefined values at the boundaries). As in our Bayesian models, day since incubation onset and covariates were z-transformed using the *scale()* function in R prior to analysis. As segmented regression cannot straightforwardly accommodate an interaction between a categorical grouping variable and the location of a breakpoint, we fitted two separate segmented mixed-effects models (one for groups without a cheat and one for groups with a cheat) rather than a single combined model. Each model estimated a single breakpoint in the effect of days since incubation onset, allowing the slope of the day effect to differ before and after the estimated breakpoint, and included the number of cooperating females and number of other females present as covariates. Group was included as the only random effect; because *nlme*, unlike *MCMCglmm*, cannot fit crossed random effects, year and camp could not be modelled as separate random terms as in our other group-level analyses. 

This analysis included `r nrow(df_activity_allocation)` observations (`r nrow(df_activity_allocation[df_activity_allocation$CheatinCamp == "No",])` in groups without cheats, and `r nrow(df_activity_allocation[df_activity_allocation$CheatinCamp == "Yes",])` in groups with cheats) of `r length(unique(df_activity_allocation$yearcamp))` groups (`r length(unique(df_activity_allocation$yearcamp[df_activity_allocation$CheatinCamp == "Yes"]))` with and `r length(unique(df_activity_allocation$yearcamp[df_activity_allocation$CheatinCamp == "No"]))` without cheats) across `r length(unique(df_activity_allocation$date))` observation days. Only data from the first 32 days of the incubation period each year were included in this analysis, and only groups where female incubation was recorded during this time were included.

Fixed effects are reported as parameter estimates with standard errors, 95% Wald-type confidence intervals, t-statistics, denominator degrees of freedom, and p-values from two-sided t-tests using the degrees of freedom estimated by *nlme.* Fixed effects were considered significant when the 95% CI did not overlap with 0 and p was less than 0.05. An exception applies to the two parameters directly describing the breakpoint itself, the change in slope (U) and the breakpoint location (G0), for which standard hypothesis testing is not valid, because the location of a breakpoint is not identifiable under the null hypothesis of no breakpoint [@davies1987]. We therefore report only point estimates and 95% CIs for U and G0, without associated p-values.
